good_story.text:
We lost our biggest client in March 2025. It was 38% of revenue.

I spent the first week refreshing my inbox, hoping they'd change their mind.

They didn't.

So we did three unglamorous things:

1. Called our 12 smallest customers and asked what they'd pay more for.
2. Raised prices on the plan nobody complained about.
3. Cut the two features only that client used.

Nine months later, revenue is up 21% and no single customer is above 9%.

The lesson I keep relearning: concentration feels like safety until the day it isn't.

If one client left you tomorrow, what would you change first?

good_howto.text:
Your pricing page loses buyers at the comparison table.

We tested 4 versions with Northwind's sales team over 6 weeks. The one that won had fewer columns, not more.

What changed:

1. Three plans instead of five. Demo requests went from 41 to 63 a month.
2. One line per plan saying who it's for, before any feature.
3. Annual price shown first, monthly in small text below.
4. The enterprise column replaced by a single 'Talk to us' link.

None of this is clever. It just removes the moment where a buyer has to do maths.

I wrote up the full test, with the before and after screenshots, as a 9-page guide.

Comment PRICING and I'll send it over.

bof_offer.text:
Acme Logistics cut onboarding from 14 days to 3.

Their ops lead, Priya, had tried two tools and a consultant before we spoke in August.

The fix wasn't software. It was a 40-minute call to map the first week, then removing 6 of the 11 steps.

If your new customers take more than a week to see value, that's usually where the money leaks.

I have 3 audit slots left in December. Book a 20-minute call through the link on my profile.
